The paper proposes a dual-denoising framework (DDLR) for inductive knowledge graph completion that addresses noise in GNN message passing through two novel sampling mechanisms: path-based sampling (using a specific scoring function) and edge-based sampling (using single-rule confidence).

**Strengths:**

Table 2 clearly demonstrates that both the path-sampling and edge-sampling modules are necessary, as removing either causes significant drops in performance across all datasets. **Weaknesses:**
The technical core of the paper contains a significant conceptual issue regarding the "remaining path score" (Eq. 9). The authors acknowledge this is an approximation because the answer entity is unknown, yet they name it "remaining path score" which misleads the reader into thinking it evaluates the structural path to the answer. In reality, it is merely a function of the current path and the query, devoid of actual knowledge about the "future" of the path. This conceptual mismatch weakens the theoretical foundation of their primary contribution. Furthermore, the statistical rigor is lacking; the paper does not report variance (standard deviation) or confidence intervals. Given the fine margins between SOTA methods in Table 1, it is impossible to know if the reported improvements are statistically significant or noise.
